title: First impressions of Hammond and the two letters
summary: Jones tells Hammond he came to see Basie, not him, and says to answer Hammond's letter about bringing Basie to New York.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band

blocks.x: How did you see John Hammond? How did you feel about him when he came in there, having enough nerve to come into a black community and interested in jazz, which was basically a black art?

My first expression to him was, 'You?'. He said, 'I'm John Hammond.' I said, 'I'm Jo Jones and this is Dick Wilson. What are you coming here to see me for. You want to see Count Basie; you don't want to see me.' And he came to me; he did not go to Basie to talk anything. I said, 'Now you don't impress me as being a Great White Father.' At that particular time I did not know that he knew something about my background. This was in 1936, but John knew about my background in 1930.
What did he do for you?
I don't know, you know how people go around and find out about the background of people's lives.
What I'm trying to say, was he instrumental in doing something for you?
Very much, because I said the letter^ one letter was from Charlie Barnet. The other letter was from John. I looked at it; I said, 'Answer this man, Basie.'
Well, what did the letter say, Jo?
He was interested in bringing Basie into New York.
